views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue engaging in the ongoing 90-day negotiation window in good faith, pressing for progress on the January talks in Beijing and readying concrete purchase commitments to keep the truce from collapsing. We should hold the line against escalation — raising tariffs or retaliating further would hand Washington the justification to let the suspended 25% tariff hike take effect in March, which our slowing economy cannot absorb. Prioritize locking in the de-escalation already underway rather than forcing confrontation.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is genuinely high, not existential. Roughly $250B of our exports face US Section 301 tariffs (timeline: List 1-3 by 2018-09-24), the Huawei CFO's arrest on a US extradition request and our own detention of two Canadians (2018-12-01 and 12-10) signal firm-level and non-tariff targeting, and the real economy is already cooling — the official manufacturing PMI contracted to 49.4 in December, the first sub-50 reading since 2016, with export orders falling for a seventh straight month (CNBC, 2018-12-31). This sits squarely at the CHN +0.5 anchor (major export sectors hit, firm-level targeting, export-hub risk) — but the December 1 G20 truce (tariffs held at 10% rather than rising to 25% on Jan 1) and the resumed Jan 7 talks show there is a live off-ramp, so ~+0.45. The action stance is mild de-escalation/engage: the truce gives us time, escalation would trigger the much worse 25% hike while our PMI is contracting, and we can trade purchase commitments (already promised at Buenos Aires) for a continued pause without capitulating on the structural IP/industrial-policy issues that would threaten our tech-independence goals. Negotiating now, in line with the restored talks, is the balanced play.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese exports under US Section 301 tariffs (Lists 1-3 by Sep 2018)
Dec 1 G20 truce: US holds $200B tariffs at 10%, suspending planned 25% hike Jan 1
Official manufacturing PMI contracted to 49.4 in Dec 2018 — first sub-50 since 2016; export orders down 7 straight months
Huawei CFO Meng arrest + China's detention of two Canadians = firm-level/non-tariff escalation risk
China's GDP growth slowest since GFC; domestic slowdown compounds tariff drag
Jan 7-9 Beijing talks resumed within 90-day window; structural IP issues still open

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires: Trump and Xi agree to 90-day negotiation window; Jan 1 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% suspended. Same day Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor (widely viewed as retaliation for Meng arrest).
Trade talks resume in Beijing; China discusses increased purchases; structural issues remain open.
China's official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.4 in December, first contraction since 2016; new export orders contracted for a seventh straight month to 46.6.
Trump holds $200B tariffs at 10%; if no deal in 90 days, 10% tariffs will rise to 25%. China agreed to buy a 'substantial' amount of US products.
